content: Erythema nodosum is an inflammatory condition that manifests as tender, red nodules located beneath the skin. These nodules are most commonly found on the shins but can also appear on other areas of the body, such as the buttocks, calves, ankles, thighs, and arms. The lesions initially present as flat, firm, warm, red, and painful lumps, typically about an inch in diameter. Over the course of a few days, these nodules may take on a purplish hue and, over several weeks, fade into brownish, flat patches. Additional symptoms associated with erythema nodosum may include fever, a general feeling of malaise, joint pain, redness or irritation of the skin, and swelling in the affected areas. The inflamed skin may eventually take on a bruise-like appearance as it resolves. In approximately half of the cases, the exact cause of erythema nodosum remains unknown. However, it can be associated with various factors, including infections, pregnancy, sensitivity to certain medications, and other underlying disorders. Common infections linked to erythema nodosum include streptococcal infections (the most frequent cause), cat scratch disease, chlamydia, coccidioidomycosis, hepatitis B, histoplasmosis, leptospirosis, mononucleosis (caused by Epstein-Barr virus), mycobacterial infections, mycoplasma, psittacosis, syphilis, tuberculosis, tularemia, and yersinia infections. Medications that may trigger erythema nodosum include amoxicillin and other penicillins, sulfonamides, sulfones, oral contraceptives, and other antibiotics. Additionally, conditions such as leukemia, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, rheumatic fever, Behçet's disease, and ulcerative colitis have been associated with this condition. Erythema nodosum is more commonly observed in women than in men. Diagnosis is primarily based on the clinical appearance of the skin nodules. A punch biopsy of a nodule may reveal characteristic histological changes, such as septal panniculitis. Additional diagnostic tests, such as a throat culture, may be performed to rule out streptococcal infection, while a chest X-ray may be used to exclude sarcoidosis or tuberculosis. If symptoms of erythema nodosum develop, it is important to schedule an appointment with a healthcare provider. Urgent medical care may not always be necessary, but timely evaluation is recommended. Treatment involves identifying and addressing the underlying cause, whether it is an infection, medication, or associated disease. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can help alleviate symptoms. Oral potassium iodide (SSKI) solutions may lead to rapid resolution of the nodules. In cases of acute inflammation, corticosteroids or salicylate medications may be required. Pain management may involve the use of analgesics and activity limitation. Topical therapies are generally not necessary, although hot or cold compresses may provide symptomatic relief. Erythema nodosum is typically not a dangerous condition, though it can be uncomfortable. Symptoms usually resolve within approximately six weeks, but recurrence is possible.
